lead: Sampling a signal makes copies of its spectrum every f_s hertz. If the signal has energy above f_s/2, neighbouring copies overlap and a high-frequency component appears at a low frequency. That false low frequency is an alias, and no digital processing after sampling can tell it from a real low tone. The cure is an analog anti-aliasing filter placed before the sampler, with cutoff at or below f_s/2. Every audio codec, ADC card and software-defined radio uses this filter, because once an alias is sampled it stays in the data.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for the sampling theorem and spectrum copies, and Unit 3 for the ideal low-pass response.

blocks.text: A sampler multiplies x(t) by an impulse train of period T_s = 1/f_s. In frequency, this repeats the spectrum X(f) at multiples of f_s.

blocks.where: X_s(f) is the spectrum of the sampled signal; X(f) is the spectrum of x(t); f_s is the sampling rate in Hz; k is any integer.

blocks.text: When X(f)=0 above f_s/2, the copies do not overlap. A low-pass filter with cutoff f_s/2 rebuilds the signal, as in Chapter 5.1.

When a component sits at f_max > f_s/2, the copies overlap. For f_s/2 < f_max < f_s, the copy centred at f_s reaches down to f_s − f_max inside the baseband, and that copy adds to the baseband spectrum. For f_max ≥ f_s, the alias comes from a different copy; take the nearest multiple of f_s, as the folding rule below does. The condition f_s < 2 f_max is exactly when this overlap starts. The overlap is aliasing; some syllabi call it fold-over. It is a permanent mixing, not a rounding error.
After sampling, every frequency f appears as the frequency nearest to zero among |f − k f_s|, for integer k. That is the folding rule.
Take f_s=1000 Hz. A 700 Hz tone is above f_s/2=500 Hz. Its nearest multiple is 1000 Hz, so the alias is |700−1000|=300 Hz. The identity below shows why.

blocks.where: n is the sample index; the sample times are t = n/1000 s; the two continuous-time cosines cos(2π·700t) and cos(2π·300t) give these same samples.

blocks.text: So cos(2π·700t) and cos(2π·300t) give identical samples at 1000 Hz. After sampling they are indistinguishable. A 1300 Hz tone also folds to 300 Hz, because |1300−1000|=300 Hz.
An anti-aliasing filter is an analog low-pass filter placed before the sampler. It removes components above f_s/2 before they can fold. Some syllabi call it a prefilter.

Choose cutoff f_c with f_max ≤ f_c ≤ f_s/2. A cutoff f_c = 2 f_max is wrong only when it exceeds f_s/2; the hard constraint is f_c ≤ f_s/2. If 2 f_max ≤ f_s/2, that cutoff is allowed but not necessarily a good design. The transition band runs from f_max to f_s/2, so its width is Δf = f_s/2 − f_max.

blocks.where: |H(f)| is the magnitude response of an N-th order Butterworth low-pass filter; f_c is the cutoff in Hz; N is the filter order.

blocks.text: The order N follows from the stopband attenuation A in dB and Δf. Solve for N from the attenuation at the stopband edge. Large A and small Δf need high N.

No digital filter after the sampler can remove an alias. The sampler has already merged the two frequencies, and the digital filter sees only the merged value. Sampling faster after an alias is equally useless; the alias is already in the samples.

figure.caption: At 1000 Hz the 700 Hz cosine and the 300 Hz cosine pass through the same points at every integer sample index. The plot shows why the samples alone cannot tell the two tones apart.

spec.aria: A 700 Hz cosine and a 300 Hz cosine meet at every integer sample index when the sampling rate is 1000 Hz.

examples.question: A speech signal occupies 300 Hz to 3400 Hz and is sampled at 8000 Hz. Is it safe from aliasing, and what guard band remains? A tone cos(2π·700t) volts is then sampled at 1000 Hz. Find the frequency of the reconstructed tone. Which other tone gives the same samples?
steps: For the speech, f_max = 3400 Hz. The Nyquist rate is 2 f_max = 6800 Hz. The given f_s = 8000 Hz is greater than 6800 Hz, so the speech does not alias.
The Nyquist frequency is f_s/2 = 8000/2 = 4000 Hz. The guard band is 4000 − 3400 = 600 Hz.
For the tone, f_s = 1000 Hz, so f_s/2 = 500 Hz. The tone frequency 700 Hz is greater than 500 Hz, so it aliases.
Fold 700 Hz to the nearest multiple of 1000 Hz. |700 − 1000| = 300 Hz. The reconstructed tone is cos(2π·300t) volts with the same amplitude, 1 V.
A tone at 1300 Hz gives |1300 − 1000| = 300 Hz, so it produces the same samples as the 700 Hz tone.
examples.answer: At f_s = 8000 Hz, f_s/2 = 4000 Hz; the speech band is safe with a 600 Hz guard band; the 700 Hz tone is reconstructed as cos(2π·300t) volts, and a 1300 Hz tone gives the same samples.
examples.check:
fs_speech = 8000
f_high = 3400
nyquist = fs_speech / 2
guard = nyquist - f_high
fs_tone = 1000
f_tone = 700
alias = abs(f_tone - fs_tone)
same_alias_tone = fs_tone + alias
print(nyquist)
print(guard)
print(alias)
print(same_alias_tone)

traps: Saying the anti-aliasing cutoff must be 2 f_max; the cutoff is at most f_s/2.
Placing the anti-aliasing filter after the sampler; it is then a digital filter and the alias is already present.
Thinking a faster sampler removes an alias that is already in the samples; the overlap has already happened.
Forgetting that for a single isolated tone the alias keeps the amplitude; for a general signal, overlapping aliases add complexly and can change the amplitude.

Measuring the transition width to f_c instead of the stopband edge; for a filter whose stopband edge is f_s/2 the transition width equals the guard band f_s/2 − f_max, and a lower stopband edge changes it.

quiz.a: Aliasing is the overlap of spectral copies when a signal above f_s/2 is sampled, so a high frequency appears as a low frequency.

quiz.q: Why must the anti-aliasing filter be analog and placed before the sampler?
quiz.a: After sampling, the alias is already merged with the wanted band; no digital filter can separate them. The analog filter removes the high frequency before the sampler creates the copy.

quiz.q: A tone cos(2π·900t) volts is sampled at 1000 Hz. Find the observed frequency and the amplitude.
quiz.a: f_s/2 = 500 Hz, and 900 > 500, so the alias is |900 − 1000| = 100 Hz. The amplitude stays 1 V; the output is cos(2π·100t) volts.

quiz.q: A signal occupies 0 to 4 kHz and is sampled at 10 kHz. Find f_s/2 and the guard band; give a valid anti-aliasing cutoff.
quiz.a: f_s/2 = 10/2 = 5 kHz. The guard band is 5 − 4 = 1 kHz. Any cutoff from 4 kHz to 5 kHz works, for example 4.5 kHz.

quiz.q: At f_s = 1000 Hz, which frequencies give the same samples as a 700 Hz tone? Give two.
quiz.a: 700 Hz folds to 300 Hz. Frequencies 300 Hz, 1300 Hz, 1700 Hz and 2300 Hz all give |f − k·1000| = 300 Hz. Two examples are 300 Hz and 1300 Hz.

quiz.q: A 3400 Hz tone is sampled at 6800 Hz. Is it safe? What happens at f_s = 6000 Hz?
quiz.a: At 6800 Hz, f_s/2 = 3400 Hz, so the tone is exactly at the limit; a practical design needs a guard band. At 6000 Hz, f_s/2 = 3000 Hz, so the tone folds to |3400 − 6000| = 2600 Hz.
The observed frequency is the distance from f to the nearest multiple of f_s: min_k |f − k f_s|.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real ADCs, anti-aliasing is split between an analog filter and oversampling. Sigma-delta converters sample at many times f_s and decimate digitally, which relaxes the analog filter. Software-defined radios put a tracking filter before the ADC because strong out-of-band transmitters would otherwise fold onto weak channels. Search for oversampling, sigma-delta ADC, decimation, and analog front end anti-aliasing.
